Scholaratalyst: A Benchmark for
Retrieving Papers that Inspire New Research

Sohyeon Kim   Yoonho Lee   Bo Liu    Dayoon Ko    Rulin Shao Affiliation:  Stanford University   Seoul National University   University of Washington    Seungone Kim    Graham Neubig    Pang Wei Koh    Aakanksha Chowdhery Affiliation:  Stanford University   Seoul National University   University of Washington    Akari Asai    Omar Khattab    Yejin Choi    Gunhee Kim    Chelsea Finn Affiliation:  Carnegie Mellon University   Allen Institute for AI   MIT
Abstract

What makes great scientists great? Even as AI systems start to make progress on open problems, scientists remain far ahead of them at sensing which prior idea, buried in an ever-growing archive of research, a new problem needs. To study this skill, we draw on researchers who know firsthand which earlier work advanced their completed projects, with papers serving as pointers to the ideas within. Using our automated pipeline that makes author annotation scalable, we build ScholarCatalyst by having 184 lead authors of 207 recent computer science papers label which candidates did or could have advanced their project, each with a detailed rationale. We introduce a retrieval task with author-provided judgments: given an initial research question, retrieve these papers from only the literature available when the project began. Agentic search does no better than embedding retrieval (0.42 vs. 0.48 Recall@20) despite calling that same retriever as a tool. Even an agent built on Claude Fable 5.1, which may have seen the completed papers during training, reaches only 0.51 R@20. These results highlight the need for new training recipes that equip models with expert intuition for searching broad corpora. We envision ScholarCatalyst as a step toward scientific agents that can take a half-formed idea and point to the prior research it needs.

1 Introduction

To invent is to discern, to choose.— Henri Poincaré

Scientific research is inherently cumulative, with each project building on previous results and ideas. Current AI systems for research mainly accelerate progress on an already well-defined subproblem, where the remaining work is closer to engineering. Deciding which existing idea a new problem should build on is still mostly left to human researchers. An insightful prior paper can turn a vague question into a well-defined problem, for instance by revealing a limitation that motivates a new direction or suggesting an approach worth adapting, thereby shaping and accelerating—catalyzing—subsequent research. Making this choice well is a defining ability of great scientists, and a critical part of what researchers call research taste. We ask whether models can make that decision through a concrete task: given an early-stage research question, find its catalyst papers, by which we mean prior papers whose ideas did or could have meaningfully advanced the project (Figure 1).

Evaluating this retrieval task requires ground truth about which papers were catalysts for a particular project. Published papers record the outcomes of completed projects, but the ideation that shaped them is largely undocumented, and bibliographies rarely distinguish the sources that provided non-obvious, critical insights from the broader set of cited works. Existing scientific retrieval benchmarks (Table 1) evaluate facet-level similarity or relevance to a stated information need (Wadden et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023; Ajith et al., 2024; Asai et al., 2024) or derive positives from citation-intent annotations for queries that withhold the eventual method (Garikaparthi et al., 2025). These signals do not capture whether a retrieved paper could have inspired an early-stage project, especially when it was not cited by the eventual paper.

We introduce ScholarCatalyst, a literature inspiration retrieval benchmark grounded in researchers’ firsthand knowledge of their own projects. 184 researchers who led 207 recent computer science projects verified 894 research questions as they stood before each project’s key findings, then labeled which prior papers did or could have advanced their work and explained why, including papers they had not encountered at the time. Given a question, a system must rank these papers near the top of a 191K-paper corpus restricted to work published before the project, using models whose knowledge cutoffs predate every source paper. This knowledge is rarely documented, and we collect it efficiently and at scale through an automated pipeline that only needs a paper’s arXiv ID to produce author-reviewable draft data. Because any newly published paper can become a fresh instance, the pipeline keeps ScholarCatalyst ahead of model training cutoffs and lets the benchmark grow with the literature.

Across sparse, dense, and multi-vector retrievers and LLM search agents, the strongest system recovers only 48% of gold (i.e., author-credited) papers in its top 20. We find that topical similarity is a weak signal: catalyst papers are no more similar to the query than related papers the authors rejected. Every search an agent issues still goes through a similarity-based retriever, so repeated querying does not help (42% vs. 48% for the retriever alone). We also evaluate Claude Fable 5.1 as a lenient upper reference because its training data may include the source papers or secondary sources describing them, and even with this advantage it misses nearly half of the gold papers in its top 20. More broadly, our results point to the need for retrieval models with an expert-level sense of which ideas matter, and ScholarCatalyst offers a way to measure progress toward them.

2 Related Work

Scientific discovery using LLMs.

Accelerating science is a major opportunity for LLM-based agents, which increasingly can propose relevant hypotheses and research ideas (Wang et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). We deliberately ground our task in existing papers. Unlike a newly generated idea, which cannot be verified without running it (Si et al., 2025; Si et al., 2026), a published paper comes with a record of what worked, why, and where it fell short. The same grounding is what lets us collect ground truth, since authors can judge existing papers against what actually advanced their project. Existing scientific-discovery systems likewise draw on prior papers, either starting from a seed or target paper and exploiting its citation graph or metadata (Wang et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2025), while others search a task-specific candidate corpus constructed in advance (Wang et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2026). Recent work studies how LLMs can generate scientific insights by combining existing ideas (He-Yueya et al., 2026), further motivating the need to evaluate which prior work agents choose to draw on. ScholarCatalyst directly addresses this evaluation gap by testing whether scientific agents can retrieve insightful prior ideas for an early-stage research question, guided by project authors’ firsthand experience of what helped their research.

Scientific literature retrieval.

Existing scientific retrieval benchmarks evaluate how well systems find evidence for claims (Wadden et al., 2020; Wadden et al., 2022), retrieve documents for specified facets (Mysore et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023), and locate papers given document context or explicit information needs (Ajith et al., 2024; Asai et al., 2024; He et al., 2025; Park et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2025). Whereas existing benchmarks provide a retrieval objective that is explicit in the query, we pose an open-ended problem that requires inferring the latent scientific relevance of papers to an early-stage research idea. MIR (Garikaparthi et al., 2025) comes closest, since its queries also withhold the project’s eventual method, but it derives positives from citation-intent annotations indicating methodological influence (Lauscher et al., 2022). Rather than inferring relevance from the published record, we elicit directly from paper authors otherwise undocumented data about the research process behind it, including early-stage research questions and relevance judgments. To our knowledge, ScholarCatalyst is the first scientific literature retrieval benchmark grounded in authors’ firsthand accounts of their research process.

Information retrieval systems.

Lexical retrievers (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) and embedding retrievers rank corpus papers through term overlap or learned semantic similarity (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Khattab and Zaharia, 2020; Zhang et al., 2025b; Shanbhogue et al., 2026). For a given query, these methods rank the corpus once and do not adapt the search to the returned papers. Search agents use LLM reasoning to iteratively formulate queries and invoke these retrievers as tools over multiple turns, enabling more adaptive search for complex information-seeking tasks (Yao et al., 2022; Jin et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). Deep research systems extend this approach with subquestion decomposition, reading, and reflection over longer horizons (Team et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a). However, these agents still access the corpus through a retriever’s top-kk candidates at each step. Recent work instead gives agents direct access to the raw corpus through terminal tools such as grep and file reads, letting the language model determine how to search and interpret documents (Li et al., 2026; Sen et al., 2026). Whether such agentic search approaches can retrieve prior work whose scientific inspiration is latent rather than lexically explicit remains unclear.

3 ScholarCatalyst: Evaluating Scientific Literature Retrieval with Authors’ Firsthand Accounts

ScholarCatalyst evaluates whether retrieval systems can identify catalyst papers, prior work whose ideas could inspire and help advance an early stage of research. To obtain firsthand judgments about inspiration, we ask project authors which prior papers did or could have helped advance their project and why, knowledge that is largely absent from the public record. We first define the task of retrieving useful prior work, including its query types, retrieval corpus, and evaluation metrics (Section 3.1). We then describe our pipeline that supports effective and efficient data collection (Section 3.2) and the subsequent author validation and revision process for finalizing the benchmark instances (Section 3.3).

3.1 Task Definition

Given a query qq from the authors of the source paper SS, the task is to retrieve catalyst papers 𝒟q+\smash{\mathcal{D}^{+}_{q}} from 𝒫<S\smash{\mathcal{P}_{<S}}, where 𝒫<S\smash{\mathcal{P}_{<S}} is a corpus containing papers published before source paper SS was completed. For each query qq, we also provide hard-negative documents, 𝒟q−⊂𝒫<S\smash{\mathcal{D}^{-}_{q}\subset\mathcal{P}_{<S}}, which are related to qq but did not inspire the authors of SS.

Each query qq is a short paragraph that reconstructs the research landscape at the outset of the project underlying the source paper SS. It describes what was known, what remained unresolved, and the open question the authors set out to answer, without revealing the eventual solution. Specifically, we consider two query types that reflect how an early-stage project develops from a broad central research question into particular subfields, with an inspiring paper potentially shaping the next step at either stage.

  • •

    A core research query (CoreQ) asks which prior ideas could help address the project’s central research question.

  • •

    A subfield-specific query (SubQ) approaches the same research question from a particular research subfield, asking which prior ideas could help advance the project from that perspective.

Figure 2 shows an example ScholarCatalyst instance (q,𝒟q+,𝒟q−)(q,\smash{\mathcal{D}^{+}_{q}},\smash{\mathcal{D}^{-}_{q}}) derived from source paper SS. For each query qq, the positive paper set 𝒟q+⊆𝒫<S\smash{\mathcal{D}^{+}_{q}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{<S}} contains papers that authors judge to offer inspiration for pursuing qq. The hard-negative set 𝒟q−⊆𝒫<S∖𝒟q+\smash{\mathcal{D}^{-}_{q}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{<S}\setminus\mathcal{D}^{+}_{q}} contains papers that the authors reviewed and rejected. Every hard-negative paper is topically related to qq, since it was either cited in SS or ranked highly for qq by a retriever.

By making the retrieval corpus 𝒫<S\smash{\mathcal{P}_{<S}} contain only papers published before SS (Yetisgen-Yildiz and Pratt, 2008; Yetisgen-Yildiz and Pratt, 2009; Halawi et al., 2024), we approximate the literature available during the research process. We also disable external web access to prevent retrieval of subsequent writing about the project and the source paper. We evaluate retrieval performance using Recall@NN, which measures the fraction of positive papers retrieved in the top NN results, and normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG@NN) (Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002), which additionally rewards higher rankings of positive papers.

3.2 Our Automated Pipeline for Efficient Data Collection

We build an automated data construction pipeline that only requires a source paper’s arXiv ID and produces the materials required for author annotation. The pipeline let us collect author-validated data at scale. It also makes it easy to refresh ScholarCatalyst with newly published papers as older instances go stale due to leakage into newer models’ training data.

Source-paper and corpus processing. For each source paper SS, we use the arXiv API11 1 https://info.arxiv.org/help/api/index.html to obtain metadata and source files, parse the full text into a structured representation, and resolve bibliography entries to canonical scholarly records. The resulting one-hop citation graph links inline citations to the referenced papers’ metadata and abstracts. Our retrieval corpus 𝒫\mathcal{P} contains 190,896 papers. It combines references resolved from our source papers with 181K additional arXiv papers from 2020–2024 across major computer-science categories. Scoping 𝒫\mathcal{P} to computer science and the source papers’ publication years keeps the corpus relevant to ScholarCatalyst without indexing all of arXiv, which now exceeds 3 million articles (arXiv, 2026). We show detailed corpus statistics in Section B.2.

Pre-annotation and candidate construction. We use Gemini 3.1 Pro to generate pre-annotations from the structured source paper SS and its bibliography. These include one CoreQ, several SubQs, and rationales explaining the proposed relevance of cited papers. We additionally retrieve uncited candidates with BM25 and Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009; Zhang et al., 2025b). Gemini 3.6 Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026b) reranks the pooled candidates for scientific relevance, and the pipeline retains 10 candidates per query to balance coverage of potential false negatives with a manageable author-review workload.

The resulting pre-annotations and candidates are loaded into a web interface for author review (Section 3.3). We describe the implementation details of our pipeline in Appendix E.

3.3 Collecting Relevance Supervision from Authors

We collect 207 projects from 184 researchers, each describing the intellectual path behind a source paper SS in computer science (CS) and artificial intelligence (AI), published in 2025–2026. Each project contributes one CoreQ task instance and one or more SubQ task instances, each of the form (q,𝒟q+,𝒟q−)\bigl(q,\mathcal{D}^{+}_{q},\mathcal{D}^{-}_{q}\bigr), together with a rationale for the relevance judgments.

  1. 1.

    Author recruitment. We recruit participants in two ways. We invite first authors of oral, spotlight, and award papers at major AI conferences in 2025--202622 2 ICLR 2026, ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2025, ACL 2026, CVPR 2026, CoLM 2025, and CoRL 2025.. We also reach out personally and issue an open call to first, co-first, and corresponding authors of any paper accepted at a major AI conference since 2025. More than 100 of the 207 source papers received an oral, spotlight, or award distinction. Full details of the author interface and recruitment procedures are provided in Appendix F.1.

  2. 2.

    Author validation and revision. Through a web interface, authors provide an account of the research underlying their source paper SS and assess the relevance of candidate papers, as shown in Figure 3. Starting from the pre-annotation of Section 3.2, they can validate, revise, or rewrite any component to reflect their own account of the research (Table 7 shows one validated query set). For each query qq, authors label every candidate from Section 3.2 as offering an insightful idea for pursuing qq or not, which yields the positives 𝒟q+\mathcal{D}^{+}_{q} and hard negatives 𝒟q−\mathcal{D}^{-}_{q}, and they explain each judgment. Together, these author-validated task instances constitute the benchmark’s relevance supervision.

  3. 3.

    Post-processing. We manually review all finalized task instances for consistency with the task definition, paying attention to whether queries describe the research question from an early-stage perspective. Of the 894 queries, 764 (85.5%) pass this review unchanged. In the rest, we reword a phrase that gives away the eventual solution or treats the work as complete, keeping the authors’ meaning and voice and changing nothing else.

4 Evaluation and Analysis

Our evaluation corpus of 191K computer-science papers is far smaller than the three million papers on arXiv (arXiv, 2026), among which researchers are able to find work that inspires a project. Retrieval in this corpus is therefore an easier version of the problem researchers actually face. In this section, we ask: can current retrieval systems identify the catalyst papers that inspired a project from among the many topically related papers in the corpus? If not, where do they fail?

4.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate lexical, multi-vector, dense, and agentic retrieval. We include BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) as a lexical baseline, since it performs strongly against dense models on BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021) and LongEmbed (Zhu et al., 2024), and LateOn (Sourty et al., 2026) as a multi-vector baseline. We evaluate seven dense retrievers. Qwen3-Embedding-4B and 8B (Zhang et al., 2025b) and Gemini Embedding 2 (Shanbhogue et al., 2026) are general-purpose models. SPECTER2 (Singh et al., 2022) and OpenScholar (Asai et al., 2024) are trained on scientific documents. ReasonEmbed (Chen et al., 2025) and Inf-Retriever-v1-Pro (Yao et al., 2025) are optimized for reasoning-intensive retrieval. Appendix D.1 provides extended results for further embedding retrievers.

We evaluate three search agents that represent common designs in the literature. The grep agent follows DCI-Agent-Lite (Li et al., 2026) and searches titles and abstracts with regular expressions. The tool-calling agent follows the search-then-select structure for literature search (He et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2026). The deep research agent adopts the workflow of deep research systems (OpenAI, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a): it breaks the query into subquestions and iterates over search, reading, and synthesis. The latter two agents retrieve candidates for their search queries with Gemini Embedding 2. We use GPT-4.1 (OpenAI, 2026a) and o3 (OpenAI, 2026e) as backbone models since they are among the strongest models with a knowledge cutoff (June 2024) before all source papers. To compare against a recent frontier model, we also evaluate Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic, 2026), which may have seen most source papers during training (June 2026 cutoff). Following previous work (Thakur et al., 2021; Su et al., 2025; Tchuindjo et al., 2026), we report nDCG@20 and Recall@kk (k=5,20,100k=5,20,100). Full experimental details are provided in Appendix C.

4.2 Main Results

All systems struggle to retrieve catalyst papers. Current retrievers miss most of the papers that inspired a project (Table 3). General-purpose dense retrievers perform best, yet place 39% of author-identified inspiration papers in the top 20 for CoreQ and 51% for SubQ. Scientific-document retrievers (SPECTER2, OpenScholar) trail the general-purpose models by at least 16 points on CoreQ and 27 points on SubQ at Recall@20. BM25 and LateOn trail by 15–16 points on CoreQ and 18–25 points on SubQ. Together, these results suggest that domain-specific training on citation signals does not by itself solve this task. Among the pre-cutoff systems in our main experiment, CoreQ is harder than SubQ, consistent with its longer queries and smaller, almost entirely cited positive sets (Table 2). We show later that reranking with an oracle candidate pool recovers part of this gap (Section 4.4).

Agentic search does not improve over embedding retrieval. We compare LLM search agents built on pre-cutoff models (GPT-4.1 and o3) against the strongest embedding model (Table 3). Grep-based search, despite its recent success as a lightweight alternative to embedding retrieval (Li et al., 2026; Sen et al., 2026), performs substantially worse. It finds only 8% of gold query–paper pairs during search, compared with 46% for the tool-calling agent (Figure 6).

We attribute this gap to candidate coverage, since regardless of how a model reasons, an agent can interact with the corpus only through its search queries. As the corpus scales, this constraint becomes more important because an agent can inspect only a small fraction of the corpus. Consistent with this account, agent recall rises with backbone capability yet remains close to the embedding retriever’s even for the strongest model (Figure 6). If coverage is the limiting factor, progress will require embedding retrievers that surface inspiration papers in the first place and agents that build on those results to guide further exploration. We report Fable 5.1 separately because it falls outside our knowledge cutoff, and we analyze its results, together with agent failure cases and retrieval rationales, in Sections D.3 and D.6.

4.3 Analysis of Author-Annotated Catalyst Papers

Inspiration relations are diverse and not captured by similarity. Prompting an LLM judge to classify each of the 663 key-inspiration rationales under a nine-type taxonomy (Appendix B.3), we find that authors most often credit a technique they adapted (method), empirical findings that supported a direction (evidence), an idea extended to a new setting (generalization), or a limitation that motivated a new approach (limitation), with more than one type applying to 55.8% of rationales (Figure 7). Similarity to the query does not identify these papers: measuring lexical similarity as the fraction of unique query words in a candidate’s title and abstract, and semantic similarity as cosine similarity under Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Zhang et al., 2025b), hard negatives are at least as similar to the query as positives on both measures (Table 11). This also limits agentic search, where grep and embedding tools construct the candidate pool before an agent can reason about which papers could inspire a project.

The published record does not reveal which papers inspired a project. Source-paper citations provide an incomplete signal of inspiration. 43.6% of SubQ positives are not cited by the source paper, and 67.8% of those share no references with it. Among cited papers, citation-intent labels do not identify inspirations: only 46.2% of CoreQ and 34.0% of SubQ positives carry a uses or extends label (Lauscher et al., 2022). Even given the entire finished source paper in addition to its bibliography, LLMs fail to identify catalyst papers. Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google DeepMind, 2026a) proposes candidate inspiration papers that cover only 32.2% of CoreQ positives on average and none of the key inspirations in 28.0% of instances. Sections B.3 and 12 give further details, including an instance with both uncited positives and cited hard negatives.

4.4 Analysis of Factors Behind Retrieval Performance

Stronger rerankers benefit more from better candidate coverage. To separate retrieval coverage from recognition performance, we apply LLM-based reranking to the top-KK candidates from Gemini-Embedding-2 on a randomly sampled subset of 50 CoreQ and 50 SubQ queries. We compare reranking with and without gold injection, which replaces negative candidates with positive papers missing from the set while keeping the pool size fixed. Stronger rerankers gain more in Recall@5 from gold injection (Figure 6). The growing gap suggests that candidate coverage limits how much we can benefit from stronger rerankers: their ability to select useful papers matters only when those papers enter the pool. Better retrieval could therefore yield larger gains as rerankers improve. Reranking prompts and procedures are provided in Section D.2.

Agents benefit from source context but not from fuller reading. We vary two kinds of agent context: information about the source paper and how much of each retrieved paper the agent reads. With a Gemini 3.7 Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026c) (cutoff March 2026) tool-calling agent on the 203-query cutoff split (Table 4), the source title and abstract raise Recall@20 by 0.11 for CoreQ and 0.02 for SubQ, while web search changes it by at most 0.01. The source bibliography, which contains 95% of CoreQ gold papers, raises it by 0.35. Without search tools, the model given the title and abstract reaches only 0.31 CoreQ Recall@20, below corpus search alone, so source context helps by guiding search rather than through memory. In contrast, letting a GPT-4.1 tool-calling agent read beyond abstracts on 50 queries per type changes Recall@20 by at most 0.04 (Figure 11), and the best SubQ policy still trails the retriever (0.50 versus 0.55). Together, these results suggest that the bottleneck lies in knowing what to search for rather than in understanding the papers already found, consistent with the candidate-coverage explanation above. Source information is used only in this analysis, and Sections C.3 and D.5 give details.

Query rewriting does not consistently improve retrieval. We test whether an LLM can improve retrieval by reasoning over the original research question to generate single-query expansions, multiple queries, or hypothetical abstracts (Gao et al., 2023). We evaluate these strategies on 50 queries of each type, using GPT-4.1 for generation and Gemini-Embedding-2 for retrieval. Neither single-query expansion nor multi-query generation yields a meaningful improvement, while both HyDE variants substantially reduce recall (Table 5). If the retriever’s misses were a matter of phrasing, an LLM that reads the research question should be able to recover some of them by rewording. That none of these strategies does so suggests the embedding space itself does not place inspiration papers near their queries, consistent with the similarity analysis in Section 4.3. We show prompts and implementation details in Section D.4.

5 Conclusion

We introduced ScholarCatalyst, a benchmark for one ingredient of research ability: identifying prior papers whose ideas could help a project move forward. Drawing on 184 researchers’ own accounts of what shaped their work, we capture judgments that the published record largely omits. Current systems recover only a fraction of the papers that authors credit, and agentic search does no better than embedding retrieval, largely because limited candidate coverage keeps many useful papers out of reach.

Limitations. ScholarCatalyst covers computer science papers from 2025–2026 with uneven representation across research areas (Table 8), so our findings may not transfer to other fields. Our labels are retrospective judgments by paper authors and are thus subject to hindsight. A more fundamental open question is the skyline, i.e., the performance ceiling of this task. As a point of reference, the human reference accuracy on ImageNet (94.9% top-5 (Russakovsky et al., 2015)) was later exceeded, and reannotation studies found that subsequent gains increasingly reflected the idiosyncrasies of the original labels (Beyer et al., 2020; Shankar et al., 2020). Catalyst paper retrieval is harder to audit this way, since relabeling by anyone other than the authors would be costly and would measure a different target, namely what an informed outsider can infer. Still, a preliminary comparison on one paper with three author-annotators in ScholarCatalyst found that coauthors marking only about seven positives per thread recovered 43–60% of the first author’s labels at 84–88% precision. This is well above the best system’s overall R@5 of 0.24, which suggests considerable room for improvement.

Outlook. Recent work on reasoning-intensive retrieval evaluates relevance relations that require reasoning to recognize (Xiao et al., 2024; Su et al., 2025; Tchuindjo et al., 2026). ScholarCatalyst pushes further, requiring judgments of how prior ideas could advance a research project. We see two milestones ahead. The first is expert-level retrieval, matching a domain expert’s judgment within their own field. The second is retrieval beyond any individual expert: being able to exercise that level of intuition across a breadth of fields no single researcher can follow. This breadth may be where such systems help most, since nearly half of the papers our authors credit (49.5%) come from outside their project’s subject area, and 43.6% of subfield-specific positives were never cited in the source paper. Researchers may therefore be limited more by what they have seen than by how well they judge it. The full literature makes this gap far larger than our benchmark shows: Semantic Scholar alone indexes over 225M papers (Kinney et al., 2023), compared with 190k in our corpus. What stands between current systems and both milestones is an expert-level sense of which ideas matter, and we hope ScholarCatalyst offers a starting point for developing it. If undiscovered public knowledge (Swanson, 1986) is as common as our results imply, models capable of expert judgment across fields could unlock a large backlog of progress hidden in plain sight.

Appendix A Benchmark Contributors

We are deeply grateful to the researchers who contributed to ScholarCatalyst by reviewing our reconstruction of their own work, revising the research questions and inspiration papers, and sharing the reasoning behind which prior work genuinely shaped their research. Their firsthand knowledge is the foundation of this benchmark, and we thank them for generously dedicating their time and expertise. Contributors who agreed to be acknowledged are listed below in alphabetical order.

Appendix B The ScholarCatalyst Benchmark

B.1 Benchmark Instance

ScholarCatalyst evaluates whether a retrieval system can find prior work whose ideas would have been insightful for pursuing a research project, rather than papers that are merely topically similar. Each instance is anchored in a completed source paper and pairs its central research question and distinct research directions with author-validated positive papers, topically related hard negatives, and a temporally restricted search corpus. The 207 author-validated instances contribute 894 queries: 207 core research queries and 687 subfield-specific queries. This appendix first defines the information in one benchmark instance (Section B.1), then reports the composition of the instances and corpus (Section B.2), and finally examines the kinds of inspiration relations the benchmark captures (Section B.3).

A project’s overarching question and its subfield-specific questions need not draw on the same prior work. The core research query can identify ideas that organize the project as a whole, whereas subfield-specific queries surface papers relevant to particular methodological or empirical directions. Their overlap and divergence reveal complementary forms of inspiration within a single project. Table 7 shows what this looks like for one full instance.

B.2 Dataset Statistics

The author-validated benchmark contains 207 source papers and 894 queries concentrated in machine learning and adjacent AI fields. Table 8 reports each source paper’s primary arXiv category,33 3 arXiv category taxonomy: https://arxiv.org/category_taxonomy where Other comprises stat.ML, cs.SE, cs.IR, cs.MA, cs.HC, cond-mat.mtrl-sci, cs.CE, q-bio.NC, cs.IT, cs.GR, and cs.NE. The author-validated set comprises 894 queries (207 central, 687 directional). Table 2 summarizes the query and corpus statistics.

The retrieval corpus contains 190,896 papers: resolved references cited by our source papers, together with a pool of additional arXiv papers drawn from five main computer science domains and published between 2020 and 2024. Table 9 reports the primary arXiv category of every corpus paper, and Table 10 reports its publication year.

Of the 190,896 corpus papers, 189,296 (99.2%) are sourced from arXiv44 4 https://arxiv.org directly. The remaining 1,600 papers (0.8%) come from Semantic Scholar (S2)55 5 https://www.semanticscholar.org/product/api and OpenAlex (OA) (Priem et al., 2022), used only when a cited paper could not be found on arXiv itself. Because the corpus includes every resolved reference our source papers cite, it also ends up containing a small number of papers published in 2025 or later, past the nominal collection window between 2020 and 2024. This does not cause temporal leakage: at evaluation time, we restrict each query’s search to only the papers published no later than that query’s own source paper.

B.3 Qualitative Analysis of Inspiration Relations

This section provides further detail on the analysis of author-identified inspiration in Section 4.3 and presents additional qualitative examples. To examine the inspirations captured by ScholarCatalyst beyond topical relevance, we qualitatively analyze author-provided rationales for catalyst papers. We first introduce a multi-label taxonomy of inspiration relations, and then present case studies illustrating cross-subfield transfer, the context-dependent role of prior work, and the imperfect correspondence between citation and inspiration. The authors’ accounts offer a rare view of the research process that finished papers seldom document: which prior ideas researchers found useful, and why. We find that these judgments are diverse in kind and unrelated to similarity, and that neither citations nor an LLM reading the finished paper can recover them.

Inspiration relations are diverse and not captured by similarity. Prompting an LLM judge to classify each of the 663 key-inspiration rationales under a nine-type taxonomy, we find that authors most often credit a technique they adapted (method), empirical findings that supported a direction (evidence), an idea extended to a new setting (generalization), or a limitation that motivated a new approach (limitation), with more than one type applying to 55.8% of rationales (Figure 7). Similarity to the query does not identify these papers: measuring lexical similarity as the fraction of unique query words in a candidate’s title and abstract, and semantic similarity as cosine similarity under Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Zhang et al., 2025b), hard negatives are at least as similar to the query as positives on both measures (Table 11). This also limits agentic search, where grep and embedding tools construct the candidate pool before an agent can reason about which papers could inspire a project.

Citation Status Is an Imperfect Proxy for Inspiration. Citation status and author-identified inspiration can diverge in both directions. Table 12 illustrates one source-paper instance in which two of four CoreQ positives are uncited, while two cited papers are hard negatives. The uncited positives informed the source paper’s exploration and offline-learning mechanisms, whereas the cited hard negatives are topically adjacent but did not shape its approach. This pattern also appears at scale: 43.6% of SubQ positives are not cited by the source paper, and 67.8% of those share no references with it. Even among cited papers, citation intent does not single out inspirations: only 46.2% of CoreQ and 34.0% of SubQ positives carry a uses or extends label (Lauscher et al., 2022).

Diversity of Inspiration Relations. Prior work inspires new research through diverse mechanisms, including direct method transfer, generalization to a new setting, limitations of existing work, and conceptual reframing. To characterize how a key inspiration paper shaped a target work, we define a nine-type taxonomy, given in Table 13, and prompt an LLM judge to label each core-research-query key-inspiration rationale with every type it clearly expresses. To capture the ways a single paper can shape a project, we allow each rationale to receive multiple type labels. The rationales receive 1.69 labels on average, with 55.8% receiving two or more and 12.7% receiving three or more. This pattern shows that inspiration often operates through several mechanisms at once.

Context-Dependent Roles of the Same Source Paper. A prior paper does not have a fixed role across research projects. It may offer a transferable method for one target, motivate a different line of inquiry for another, and provide little value for a third despite topical overlap. Its usefulness depends on the question a project is trying to answer. Table 15 shows one key catalyst paper, selected as a CoreQ positive by three unrelated source papers, each applying it in a different way.

Appendix C Experimental Setup

This appendix specifies the model configurations, agentic baselines, and evaluation conditions used in our experiments. Supplementary analyses are in Appendix D, and all prompts are in Appendix G.

C.1 Model Configurations

Table 16 summarizes the retrieval models used in ScholarCatalyst, including their architectures, input limits, and whether they receive a task-specific instruction. Resource links point to the corresponding checkpoint, API, or implementation. Table 17 lists the language-model backbones used for agentic search and LLM reranking. GPT-4.1 and o3 run under the knowledge-cutoff rule of Table 3; the other backbones serve the reranking, backbone-swap, and leakage analyses, and Claude Fable 5.1 also appears in the rows of Table 3 marked ‡\ddagger.

C.2 Evaluation Setup for Pre-discovery Retrieval

Our main setting is retrieval from a temporally filtered local corpus. For each query, we exclude corpus papers published after its source paper, so that the retriever can access only literature available when the project began. We disallow web search. Table 18 reports the resulting searchable corpus size per query. Although the temporal cutoff removes later work, the searchable corpus remains large, with a median of 190,574 papers across both query types.

C.3 Agentic Search Baselines

Shared setup.

Under the main setting, agents search a temporally filtered local corpus of paper titles and abstracts, with no access to the web or the source paper, and their backbones have knowledge cutoffs preceding all source papers. The corpus-search tool returns the ten papers the retriever ranks highest under the temporal cutoff. All calls use temperature 0, except GPT-5.6 backbones (Section D.3), which set a reasoning effort instead, and Claude Fable 5.1, which uses its default thinking setting.

Agents return rankings of different lengths, so we score each on a depth-100 list. The list starts with the agent’s ranking, adds up to 25 papers the agent saw but did not rank, in discovery order, and fills the rest with the retriever ranking of the original query, without duplicates or the source paper. The cap of 25 keeps an agent that sees many papers but ranks few from displacing the retriever back-fill. R@5 and R@20 thus come from the agent’s own ranking unless it holds fewer than kk papers, which happens mainly for the grep agent (440 of 894 queries at R@20, against 10 and 95 for the tool-calling and deep research agents, and at most 93 for any Claude Fable 5.1 row). Trajectory recall is the share of gold papers among the papers an agent sees during its run.

Tool-calling agent.

The agent combines the ReAct function-calling pattern (Yao et al., 2022), the five-round budget of PaperScout (Pan et al., 2026), and the search-then-select design of PaSa (He et al., 2025). It first searches the query as written, then runs up to 5 rounds, each one backbone reply with any number of search calls. Returned papers enter a pool of at most 60. The backbone then scores each pooled paper from 0 to 10 from its title and abstract, by how much its ideas could help a researcher pursue the query, and the scores sorted with ties in discovery order give the ranking. We do not run PaSa or PaperScout as released, because both search the web and PaperScout releases no checkpoint of its trained policy, whose base model has no vendor-stated knowledge cutoff. We omit their citation-expansion step because the corpus has no citation graph resolved to corpus papers.

Deep research agent.

The agent follows the plan, search, read, and synthesize procedure of deep research systems (OpenAI, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a), with the same search tool and o3 (OpenAI, 2026e) as backbone. It splits the query into at most 6 sub-questions, searches the query as written, then makes up to 20 searches, 10 reads, and a pool of 150 papers. A read returns the paper’s title and abstract. After every 5 calls, a reflection step asks which sub-questions remain uncovered. A final synthesis call ranks up to 50 pooled papers by usefulness, and this list is the ranking, with no per-paper judge.

Grep agent.

We re-implement DCI-Agent-Lite (Li et al., 2026), which searches the raw corpus using shell commands rather than a retriever. The released harness has read and shell tools and a 300-turn budget; ours has one shell tool, 20 rounds, and results truncated to 4,000 characters. The corpus is given as monthly files with one paper per line (identifier, title, abstract, date), and the prompt asks the agent to search abstracts with regular expressions and return an ordered list of identifiers. The backbone is GPT-4.1.

Claude Fable 5.1 rows.

We also run all three agents with Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic, 2026), which compares the procedures using a single backbone. Its June 2026 knowledge cutoff follows all but 6 of the 207 source papers, so these rows fall outside the rule of Section 4.1 and are marked in Table 3. The model’s safety classifiers sometimes decline a call, which we treat as an empty reply. Declines occur on 47 of the 894 queries for the tool-calling agent, 95 for the deep research agent, and 33 for the grep agent. About half of the deep research agent’s declines are labeled as requests for the model’s reasoning, almost all at or right after the reflection step; all others are labeled biology or cyber-security risk. A declined judge call ranks the paper after all scored papers, a declined loop turn ends the search, and a declined synthesis leaves the deep research agent with only the seen papers and the back-fill.

Analysis conditions.

The remaining conditions relax the main setting and are used only for analysis in Section D.3, not for direct comparison with the query-only agents. The last three give extra information to the tool-calling agent with Gemini 3.7 Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026c), and all are back-filled to depth 100 as above.

  • •

    Closed-book (recall-from-memory). A backbone may know the source papers’ bibliographies from training, so part of its agent’s recall could come from memory. To measure this, the backbone receives the query and the source paper’s title and abstract, has no tools, and names up to 30 prior papers. Each title is resolved to the top hit of a retriever search under the temporal cutoff, with no similarity threshold, and we drop duplicates, titles whose search returns nothing, and the source paper.

  • •

    Source paper. This measures how much the query-only restriction costs, since a real user would know more than the query. The agent’s first message includes the source paper’s title and abstract.

  • •

    Web search. This tests whether web access, where the source paper and its citations may appear, can substitute for the local corpus. The agent also gets a web-search tool (ten results per call) and a page-reading tool (pages truncated to 6,000 characters, at most five per query), and must call a tool in its first two rounds. A web result enters the pool only if its address contains an arXiv identifier or its normalized title matches a corpus paper. Other results are shown to the agent but not pooled.

  • •

    Bibliography. This gives an upper bound on what any leak of the answer could achieve. We map the source paper’s bibliography, taken from its arXiv HTML version, to corpus papers by arXiv identifier or exact title (46 of 54 entries on average). The leak upper-bound row of Table 22 adds these papers to the agent’s pool and prompt, and the bibliography-alone row ranks them in citation order without a model.

Appendix D Additional Analyses

This appendix gives details and supplementary results for our extended comparison of embedding retrievers and for the analyses of LLM reranking, knowledge cutoffs, query generation, full-text reading, and agent search failures.

D.1 Extended Results for Embedding Retrievers

This section reports extended results for a broader set of recent embedding retrievers, including models trained on scientific documents and models optimized for reasoning-intensive retrieval. Recently, several embedding retrievers have been developed for reasoning-intensive retrieval, where identifying relevant documents for complex queries requires reasoning beyond surface-level semantic matching (Xiao et al., 2024; Su et al., 2025; Tchuindjo et al., 2026). We evaluate SciNCL (Ostendorff et al., 2022), OpenScholar (Asai et al., 2024), GTE-Qwen2-7B (Li et al., 2023), ReasonEmbed (Chen et al., 2025), INF-X-Retriever (Yao et al., 2025), Llama NV-Embed-Reasoning-3B (NVIDIA, 2026), and DIVER (Long et al., 2025). Interestingly, none of the reasoning-optimized models improves over the strongest general-purpose embeddings. Their lack of gains suggests that current objectives for reasoning-intensive retrieval do not adequately capture the relationships that make a prior paper useful for advancing a research project. As discussed in Section 5, closing this gap may require an expert-level sense of which ideas matter, enabling retrieval of useful connections across fields beyond the scope of any individual expert.

D.2 LLM Reranking

We test whether an LLM can reorder the retriever’s candidates to place gold papers higher, using two procedures over candidate pools from Gemini-Embedding-2. The listwise reranker gives the top 20 candidates to a single LLM call, which returns them in ranked order. The tournament reranker handles larger pools by ranking batches of b=20b=20 papers and promoting the top k=4k=4 of each batch to the next round, until one batch remains and its ranking is the final order. Both use the prompt in Section G.2. We additionally extend the evaluation to candidate pools of K∈{20,40,80,160}K\in\{20,40,80,160\}; Tables 20 and 8 report standard and oracle reranking results across these pool sizes.

These results suggest that reranking requires recognizing which prior papers in a retrieved candidate set contain ideas that may inspire the project. Reranking performance generally improves with the backbone’s reasoning capability. Claude Fable 5.1 is the most recent backbone we evaluate and achieves the strongest results. Weaker models provide little benefit and can even underperform the retriever-only baseline on SubQ queries.

D.3 Post-cutoff Backbones and Benchmark Leakage

Setup. Our main experimental setup keeps every backbone’s knowledge cutoff before every source paper and gives the agent neither the source paper nor web access. This section asks what happens when these restrictions are lifted: whether newer backbones gain from having seen the source papers, and how much the source paper, the web, or its bibliography would help. We use two slices of the author-written set, matched by primary arXiv category. The pre-cutoff slice contains 23 source papers published between February 12 and December 23, 2025, with two cs.SE slots filled by cs.CE and cs.MA papers. The post-cutoff slice contains 23 source papers published between May 8 and August 14, 2026, four months later. A backbone whose cutoff falls between the slices can have seen the first but not the second.

The pre-cutoff slice is harder for every system (core research query retriever R@100 of 0.49 against 0.63), so we compare each system with the retriever within the same slice. Table 21 evaluates five backbones and their closed-book counterparts, and Table 22 varies the availability of access to source papers, the web, and the bibliography for Gemini 3.7 Flash.

The cutoff split shows no sign that stronger backbones gain from having seen the source papers. With GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Fable 5.1, the tool-calling agent exceeds the retriever at core research query R@20 on both slices, while the other three backbones stay close to it (Table 21). Because every system scores higher on the post-cutoff slice, we compare each backbone’s margin over the retriever within a slice. For GPT-5.6 Sol, whose cutoff falls between the slices, the margin is the same on both (0.07 and 0.06), so it shows no gain from having seen the earlier papers. Claude Fable 5.1 cannot be tested this way because its cutoff falls inside the post-cutoff slice. Closed-book recall rises with capability, but this fits memorization and general capability equally well, so it does not settle the question. At the subfield-specific query level, no agent or closed-book row exceeds the retriever on either slice.

With the same source context, search adds more to weak backbones than to strong ones. Figure 10 holds the February 2026 cutoff fixed across the GPT-5.6 family and varies capability through Luna’s reasoning effort and the model tier. Given the source abstract, the agent beats recall from memory by 0.25 for Luna at no reasoning effort, and the gap shrinks to within noise for the stronger runs. Raising Luna’s effort helps memory and hurts the query-only agent, while a stronger tier helps both. Figure 9 shows a related pattern across seven backbones: capability tracks core research query recall but not subfield-specific query recall.

The source abstract helps, web search does not, and the bibliography nearly gives away the answer. With Gemini 3.7 Flash, the source title and abstract raise core research query R@20 by 0.11 on both slices (Table 22). Web search leaves recall almost unchanged, even though the source paper appears in the web results for 85 of the 203 queries. The bibliography alone contains nearly all gold papers (R@100 above 0.9). The main protocol therefore withholds the source paper, its bibliography, and the web.

D.4 Query Generation Methods

These methods test whether rewriting the research question with an LLM brings retrieval closer to the gold papers, which often use different vocabulary from the question. All use GPT 4.1, with the prompts in Section G.2 as the system message and the research question as the user message.

  • •

    Single-query expansion. The model’s output, the question plus a short continuation, replaces the question as the retrieval query.

  • •

    Multi-query generation. The model returns up to five augmented questions, each used as a separate retrieval query. Their top-1,000 rankings are fused with reciprocal rank fusion (kk=60, Cormack et al. (2009)).

  • •

    HyDE (Gao et al., 2023). The model writes five hypothetical abstracts of prior papers, and each is used as a retrieval query, with the rankings fused as above. Its user message is the question prefixed with Research question:.

Tables 23 and 24 show generated outputs for the same CoreQ instance from the fixed CoreQ/SubQ subset. For this instance, dense retrieval on the original question recovers a gold paper that the generated queries do not recover in their top 100 results. Table 23 shows the original question alongside single- and multi-query generation. Table 24 shows three hypothetical abstracts generated by HyDE for the same question.

D.5 Reading Full Papers versus Abstracts

Agents in the main setting see only titles and abstracts. An abstract states a paper’s main result but often omits other critical details, so a gold paper could look unrelated to the question from its abstract alone. Indexing full text is not a simple fix, since embedding-based retrievers handle long documents poorly (Zhu et al., 2024) and a paper’s body far exceeds the input length they are trained on. We therefore keep search over abstracts and instead let the agent read more of the papers it finds, testing whether that extra text helps it judge and pursue candidates.

Full-text subset.

Full text is available for 180,399 corpus papers, converted from arXiv HTML, LaTeX source, or PDF and split by section heading. A query qualifies when all of its gold papers have full text. A source paper enters the subset when its CoreQ qualifies and at least one of its SubQ does, giving 158 CoreQ and 403 SubQ. We sample 50 queries of each type, separate from the 100 queries used in the other analyses. The search tool and the back-fill are restricted to the full-text papers. Reads share the five-round budget with searches. All other settings follow that of the tool-calling agent.

Read policies.

Four policies add to the abstract the introduction, the method sections, the bibliography, or both the introduction and the bibliography. A fifth returns the full paper, and a sixth lets the agent request one section from a list returned by a second tool. Introductions are matched by their heading, methods by headings containing method, approach, model, framework, algorithm, or architecture, and bibliographies by references or bibliography. If no heading matches, the tool returns the abstract. Each read is capped at 12,000 characters, about 41% of the body at the median for papers read in full, and an included bibliography has its own 6,000-character cap.

D.6 Analysis of Agent Search Failures and Rationale Explanations

We analyze why agentic search fails to improve over retrieval, studying three possible causes in turn:

  • •

    Coverage. We measure how many gold papers agents find outside the retriever’s candidates.

  • •

    Ranking. We trace three search trajectories to see where gold papers are found and lost.

  • •

    Recognition. We check whether agents explain the gold papers they rank highly the same way the authors do.

Coverage: agents rarely find gold papers beyond the retriever’s pool. Table 26 splits gold papers by two outcomes, whether Gemini-Emb-2 retrieves them in its top 100 and whether each agent ranks them in its own top 20. The retriever’s top 100 covers 70% of gold papers, and the agents recover almost none of the rest. About half of gold papers are returned by no search during an agent’s run. The first search, which uses the query as written, accounts for about two-thirds of the gold papers an agent sees, and follow-up searches add few. The grep agent, which writes its own search commands instead of using the retriever, keeps only 8% of the gold papers the retriever covers.

Ranking: agents drop many of the gold papers they do find. Among the gold papers in the retriever’s top 100, the tool-calling and deep research agents each keep 57% and 48% in their top 20. Tables 27, 28 and 29 trace one agent’s searches and final ranking on each of three core research query queries, marking gold papers wherever a search returns them. The grep agent retrieves no gold papers in any of the three.

  1. Case A.

    Ranking failure. The retriever ranks two gold papers first and fifth, and both agents retrieve them in their first search. The tool-calling agent keeps only one in its ranking, and the deep research agent keeps neither.

  2. Case B.

    Follow-up recovery. A follow-up search by both agents finds a gold paper that the retriever ranks beyond 100.

  3. Case C.

    Query drift. The retriever’s top 30 contains three of the four gold papers. The agents’ follow-up searches narrow to a subtopic and miss them, and the deep research agent leaves the one gold paper it does retrieve out of its ranking.

Recognition: agents usually explain gold papers the way the authors do. For the gold papers an agent does rank highly, we check whether its backbone understands why they matter. For each of the 238 core research query gold papers in the tool-calling agent’s top 20, GPT-4.1 explains from the query, title, and abstract how the paper could help pursue the query, and a GPT-4.1 judge compares this explanation with the author’s rationale. Of the 219 pairs whose author rationale is long enough to compare, 76% describe the same relationship, and almost all others describe a different but valid one (Table 30). Because the same model writes and judges, this agreement is an upper estimate. The analysis also shows only that the backbone can explain a paper’s relevance once given it, not that this understanding is why the paper entered the ranking.

D.7 Cost and Search Effort of the Agents

Table 31 reports the search effort, API cost and time per query of each agent in Table 3. With GPT-4.1 and o3, the grep and deep research agents carry a growing context through 14 to 20 tool calls per query and cost about eight times as much as the tool-calling agent, which makes few searches and scores each pooled paper in a short, separate call. With Claude Fable 5.1 the tool-calling agent issues more than twice as many searches within the same five rounds, and every agent costs more than a dollar per query. Times are medians over queries run in parallel and include API latency and retries, so they vary with provider load.

Appendix E Automated Data Construction Pipeline

We construct ScholarCatalyst through an end-to-end pipeline that transforms raw arXiv papers into benchmark instances for inspiration literature retrieval. Starting from recent computer science papers, the pipeline constructs a collection of source papers, reconstructs benchmark annotations, assembles a retrieval corpus with a time cutoff, and augments benchmark instances through candidate retrieval and validation. Figure 3 summarizes the overall construction pipeline.

Existing publicly available scientific corpus (Lo et al., 2020) and kaggle arXiv datasets66 6 https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/sumitm004/arxiv-scientific-research-papers-dataset do not provide the combination of recency, full-text representation, bibliography information, and citation relations required by our setting. We therefore build directly from raw arXiv data, processing each paper into a structured representation with explicit citation links that supports all subsequent stages of benchmark construction.

E.1 Source-paper Processing

We enumerate candidate source papers from recent oral and spotlight lists for recent AI conferences, match each accepted paper to its arXiv preprint by title, and exclude surveys and review articles. For each paper, we obtain a structured representation from the arXiv HTML rendering when available and otherwise by converting the corresponding LaTeX source using LaTeXML77 7 LaTeXML project: https://math.nist.gov/~BMiller/LaTeXML/, which better preserves document structure and citation information than PDF-based processing (Frankston et al., 2024). Because some papers cannot be reliably converted due to source formatting or parsing failures, we apply quality filtering to remove papers with incomplete text or citation structure. The resulting full text is converted into a structured representation in which inline citations are replaced with explicit citation markers linked to bibliography entries, providing a citation-grounded representation for all downstream stages.

We resolve every cited reference to a canonical scholarly record using the arXiv88 8 https://arxiv.org, Semantic Scholar99 9 https://www.semanticscholar.org/product/api, and OpenAlex (Priem et al., 2022) APIs based on the bibliography text. Citation parsing, inconsistent bibliography formatting, and search engine limitations occasionally prevent reliable resolution of the intended paper. We retain only source papers for which at least 70% of cited references are successfully resolved, and discard the rest before they proceed to the remaining pipeline stages, ensuring sufficient citation coverage for annotation reconstruction.

E.2 Pre-annotation Generation

From the structured source paper, we automatically reconstruct the benchmark instances. The model (Gemini 3.1 pro) reads the full paper together with its bibliography to recover the motivating research question (query qq, one CoreQ and several SubQs), inspiration papers (positive papers Dq+D_{q}^{+}) for each query. It further generates detailed rationales explaining how each selected paper contributed to the resulting research. These annotations form the benchmark instances used throughout the evaluation. This reconstruction uses the prompts provided in Appendix G.3.

E.3 Candidate Retrieval

We augment the benchmark beyond the paper’s cited bibliography by recovering insightful papers that were not cited. For each retrieval query, we retrieve the top-15 candidate papers from the corpus using both sparse (BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009)) and dense (Qwen3 8B embeddings (Zhang et al., 2025b)) retrieval systems, deduplicate them, and rerank with a reasoning model (Gemini-3.6-flash) that scores each candidate for scientific relevance to the query rather than mere topical similarity. We retain the top 10 for author review, where authors mark inspiring papers as positives and closely related but non-inspiring papers as hard negatives.

Retrieval corpus. We construct a retrieval corpus containing 190,896 papers. The corpus includes resolved references cited by our source papers together with a pool of 181K additional arXiv papers published between 2020 and 2024, drawn from five main computer science domains (cs.CL, cs.CV, cs.LG, cs.RO, and cs.AI), each restricted to papers with at least 1 citation. To construct a realistic literature pool beyond the cited literature, we estimate the citation distribution of recent ICML, ICLR, and NeurIPS oral and highlight papers and use it to determine the publication-year and category distributions of additional corpus papers. At retrieval time, we additionally apply a per-query temporal cutoff based on the query’s source-paper publication date, restricting candidate documents to those published no later than the query paper itself. This precludes temporal leakage, ensuring that no candidate postdates the query paper it is retrieved for.

The prompts used in the pipeline are in Section G.3.

E.4 Author Validation of the Automated Pipeline

Evaluation against author judgments. The final author-written set results from authors validating and revising the pipeline’s reconstructions, enabling us to measure how closely the pipeline’s initial outputs align with author judgments. In total, 184 researchers completed the validation form for 207 source-paper instances, together reviewing 687 subfields. Table 32 summarizes the validation results across all annotation stages.

Authors rated the reconstructed CoreQ as accurate or mostly accurate for 98.1% of the 207 instances (60.9% fully accurate). The same holds for individual subfields: across all 687 subfields, the reconstructed SubQ was rated accurate or mostly accurate 95.9% of the time (64.9% fully accurate). The pipeline’s reconstructed questions thus capture what authors recall motivating their work, both for a paper as a whole and for each of its research directions.

For SubQs, the candidate step shows the value of pooling. Authors retained 85.1% of originally cited candidates as positives, making citations a high-yield starting point. More importantly, authors judged 35.1% of pooled, non-cited candidates—papers absent from the source paper’s bibliography—as genuine inspirations.

Finally, we evaluate the pipeline’s key-inspiration nomination for CoreQs. For each paper’s CoreQ, the pipeline selects cited papers as likely key inspirations. We compare these nominations with the cited papers that the author ultimately labels positive.

Model-generated dataset. Given this fidelity, we apply the pipeline to 250 additional papers to form the model-reconstructed set, yielding 250 central queries and 863 directional queries.

Appendix F Author Data Collection

F.1 Author Recruitment

We recruit first-author, co-first-author, and corresponding authors of highlighted papers (oral, spotlight, and award) at recent iterations of ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS, CVPR, CoLM, CoRL, and ACL, together with institution-wide public recruitment open to any first, co-first, or corresponding author of a paper accepted at a major AI conference from 2025 onward. Participants were invited through direct email and public calls. The recruitment page in Figure 12, and the annotation interface in Figure 13. In total, 184 authors contributed 207 author-written instances.

F.2 Annotation Interface

We developed a web-based interface through which authors annotate their own research projects. For each source paper, authors write or revise a research question intended to reflect their pre-solution information state. They organize the question into distinct research subfields and identify prior papers that provided meaningful scientific inspiration for each direction. Authors then review additional candidate papers, labeling papers that provided meaningful inspiration as positives and plausible but non-inspirational papers as hard negatives. For each judgment, they provide a rationale explaining how the paper did or did not contribute to the development of the target work. The resulting author-written instances contain research questions, positive and hard-negative labels, and open-ended rationales.
